title: N-D-R

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-D-V: nedavah, the freewill gift, so generous Moses had to ask the people to stop. Your line was free gift. What did you give? Today, change one letter, and the gift becomes a promise. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

"I'll bring the dessert on Friday, bli neder." Listen around some Jewish tables and you'll hear those two words tacked onto ordinary promises. Bli neder: without a vow. It sounds like a hedge, a way of getting out of the cake. It's the opposite. It comes from taking a vow so seriously that you don't want a casual promise about dessert to become one by accident. Today's root is the word inside that phrase, the word people would rather not say lightly.
screen: `I'LL BRING DESSERT, BLI NEDER.` → `WITHOUT A VOW.` → `NOT A HEDGE: RESPECT.`

segments.voice: N-D-R. Nun, dalet, resh. Neder: a vow, a promise made before God. Turn it three ways. First, the weight of a word. The Torah says that when someone vows a vow, "he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth." What comes out of your mouth becomes something you owe. Second, the advice. Ecclesiastes, Kohelet, the Gatherer from a few days ago, says it plainly: "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." Not a ban on vows. A warning about making them cheap. That's where bli neder comes from: a habit of guarding the word. Third, the night the vows are spoken about. The evening of Yom Kippur opens with Kol Nidre, all vows, from this root. It's a legal formula, sung slowly, that asks for release from vows a person can't keep. It's been argued over and explained in more than one way. Some read it as a mercy for the person who promised too much. Some hear in it the sound of a whole community admitting how often words outrun lives. Either way, Yom Kippur night begins not with a hymn but with the subject of promises. And yesterday's word is the neighbor here. The rabbis set the two side by side: a nedavah is a gift you hand over, a neder is a promise you take on. One letter apart, and both start with a heart that's willing. The difference is that a vow follows you out the door.
screen: `DO ALL THAT PROCEEDETH OUT OF HIS MOUTH.` · `BETTER NOT TO VOW THAN NOT TO PAY.` · `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `NEDAVAH HANDED OVER, NEDER TAKEN ON.` · then, large: `A VOW FOLLOWS YOU OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one vow. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a promise you've made that's still open. Not a grand one. I'll call you back. I'll read it this week. I'll be there Saturday. Notice the ones that slipped. Don't punish yourself for them. Just choose one promise you can actually keep, and keep it soon. Picture yourself doing it: the call, the visit, the finished thing. Let your word and your day line up again. If you pray, you can bring that promise into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
screen: `AN OPEN PROMISE.` · `CHOOSE ONE YOU CAN KEEP.` · `PICTURE IT DONE.`

segments.voice: N-D-R. Nun, dalet, resh: the root of neder, a vow, and of Kol Nidre, all vows. Today's word.
Your line: vow. Today, keep the one promise you chose, and make the next one carefully, or not at all. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Some Jews add bli neder, 'without a vow', to everyday promises so they won't become binding vows, and the evening service of Yom Kippur begins with Kol Nidre, a formula about the release of vows.

fork.setup: a friend asks if you'll bring dessert on Friday. you plan to, but you're careful with your word. what do some Jews add?
fork.reveal: bli neder: a promise kept as a promise, without becoming a vow. taking vows seriously means not making them by accident.

original.note: Hebrew: a vow, from the root nun, dalet, resh.

trapdoor: what you thought: a vow is just a big promise.
what it means: a neder binds what comes out of your mouth, so carefully that people add bli neder to small promises.
what a scholar hears: Numbers 30 governs vows; Ecclesiastes 5 warns against unpaid vows; the rabbis distinguish neder and nedavah.

notes: Numbers 30:2 and Ecclesiastes 5:5 quoted from KJV (KJV numbering; JPS 30:3 and 5:4). Confirm wording and verse numbers.
Kol Nidre described as a legal formula for release from vows, sung on Yom Kippur evening, 'argued over and explained in more than one way'; no dates or history claims.

Neder vs nedavah: the Mishnah (Kinnim 1:1; Megillah 1:6) distinguishes a neder ('I take upon myself', obligation persists if the animal is lost) from a nedavah ('this one'). Paraphrased loosely as 'a gift you hand over, a promise you take on'. Confirm.
'One letter apart' refers to N-D-V vs N-D-R (vet vs resh); not an etymological claim.
howItsDone says 'Some Jews add bli neder': general usage claim; soften to 'Some Jews' if the Keeper prefers.
